info.rowActions: “Use this one” makes this configuration the active one — the Active badge marks it, and AI features always use the active configuration. “Change model” fetches the model list from the endpoint so you can pick one. “Duplicate” copies the configuration together with its stored key — useful for trying a second model side by side. “Rename” changes the label shown in this list. “Delete” removes the endpoint, the stored key and the model; AI features stop if it was the active configuration.
info.reasoning: Asks the model to answer without a separate reasoning phase, which saves time and tokens. Leave it on for most providers. Turn it off only if the endpoint rejects the request (for example a direct OpenAI URL).
info.slowModel: Gives this connection much longer to answer: an hour for a whole reply, and fifteen minutes before the first token. Turn it on for a local model server that thinks for minutes before it answers. Leave it off for a hosted provider, where a long silence means the connection is dead and should fail quickly. The long limits only apply when a worker runs the recommendation ticks — a web request is cut off by the web server long before them.
info.maxBatchSize: The most articles one request may ask the model to score. A shorter list is easier for a small model to keep in order, and it limits what one runaway reply can cost — a 4B local model given 45 articles per batch answered eight batches correctly, then lost its place on the ninth and kept inventing ids until it ran out of room to reply. The taste history is re-sent with every batch, though, so a lower cap also means more requests and more prompt tokens over the whole run. Leave it empty to use the default of {{default}}.
info.batchConcurrency: How many batch requests one run sends at the same time (1–8). A hosted provider usually copes with 4–8 and finishes a run faster; a local model server is often best at 1. Lower it if the provider rate-limits you.
info.modelPicker: The list is fetched live from this configuration's endpoint. Pick the model AI features should use — the configuration is ready once a model is saved.
info.name: A free label for this configuration, shown only in this list. Leave it empty to show the endpoint's host instead.
info.baseUrl: The root URL of an OpenAI-compatible API, including the version path — for example https://api.openai.com/v1 for OpenAI itself, or the address of a local server such as LM Studio. Any provider that speaks the OpenAI chat API works.
info.apiKey: Optional — a local model server such as LM Studio or Ollama needs no key, so you may leave the field empty. The key is sent to the server once and stored encrypted; it is never shown again. Afterwards the list only shows its last characters so you can tell keys apart. Enter a new key to replace the stored one.
info.autoGenerate: How often a new “For you” run starts on its own. The schedule needs the background worker (Docker) or the maintenance cron — without one, nothing starts by itself and a note appears below with the call to trigger runs externally. “Only manually” disables the schedule; you can always start a run yourself.
info.lookback: How many days back a run looks for candidate articles. Only unread articles inside this window are considered; “Maximum articles” caps how many of them one run may take.
info.guidance: Your own steering text for the picks — topics to prefer, topics to avoid, tone. It is sent on top of the fixed prompt below. Leave it empty to use the built-in default (shown as the placeholder); “Reset to default” clears your text.
info.profile: What the model has distilled from your reading to steer its picks. It is read-only and refreshes as your taste shifts; clear the list from Diagnostics if you want it rebuilt.
info.showReasons: Adds a one-line reason under each recommended article, explaining why the model picked it, together with the score it gave. Turn it off for a cleaner list; both are produced either way, this only controls whether they are shown.
info.favoritesCap: How many of your most recently favorited articles are shown to the model as taste history. 0 leaves favorites out.
info.keptCap: How many of your most recently kept articles are shown to the model as taste history. 0 leaves kept articles out.
info.viewedCap: How many of your most recently viewed articles are shown to the model as taste history. 0 leaves viewed articles out.
info.candidatePool: The upper bound on unread articles one run considers, taken newest-first inside the look-back window. A larger pool sees more of your backlog but costs more tokens and time.
info.picksLimit: How many recommendations one run may produce at most.
info.batchCount: How the candidate pool is split into requests. Empty means automatic: the run packs as many articles per request as the context window allows. A fixed number forces exactly that many batches — useful when a provider struggles with large requests.
info.contextWindow: The token budget one request may use. The line below says where the current value comes from: your override here, the limit your provider reports, or the built-in default. Leave the field empty to use the provider value or the default.
info.fixedPrompt: The role and output contract every run sends. They are fixed so the response stays machine-readable — the guidance prompt above is the place for your own instructions.
info.debug: When on, every run keeps its full request and response log. The log appears in the “Debug log” panel below once a run has produced entries. Debug mode does not change what the recommendation list shows — that is what “Show why articles were picked” controls.
info.purge: Deletes every recommended article from “For you” for this account. The articles themselves and their read state stay untouched. This cannot be undone — the next run builds a fresh list.

guide.title: Step-by-step setup
guide.intro: Two short walkthroughs: connect an AI endpoint first, then tune the “For you” recommendations.
guide.connectionStep2: Enter the endpoint of an OpenAI-compatible API — for example https://api.openai.com/v1.
guide.connectionStep3: Enter the API key for that endpoint.
guide.connectionStep4: Press “Add configuration”, then fetch the model list with “Change model” and save a model.
guide.connectionStep5: Press “Use this one” to make the configuration active.
guide.recommendationsStep1: Confirm the active configuration is ready. It shows a model, and the “Recommendations” card below reports that AI features are available.
guide.recommendationsStep2: Choose a capable model. qwen3.7-flash is a good default — it gives a strong quality-to-price ratio. Set it on the active configuration with “Change model”.
guide.recommendationsStep3: Pick an auto-generate schedule, or keep “Only manually”. A schedule needs the background worker or the maintenance cron.
guide.recommendationsStep4: Optional: open “Expert settings” to adjust the history caps, the article and pick limits, and the guidance prompt.
guide.recommendationsStep5: Save. Turn on Debug mode to inspect the next run in the debug log.

passkeyHelp.label: How do I find these values?
passkeyHelp.idIntro: A browser uses a passkey only on the domain it was made for. Write the domain on its own: no https://, no port, no path.
passkeyHelp.rule1: It must be the host you serve from, or a parent of it. example.com works for reader.example.com. It does not work for other.com.
passkeyHelp.rule2: A public suffix is refused. You cannot own com or co.uk.
passkeyHelp.rule3: An IP address is refused. Use a domain name. localhost is the one exception.
passkeyHelp.rule4: Passkeys need a secure page. Use HTTPS, or localhost.
passkeyHelp.idWarning: Changing the domain signs out every passkey, permanently. The domain is written into each passkey when it is made, so an existing one stops matching and cannot be repaired. The reader refuses the change until you confirm it, then deletes the passkeys it made unusable. Each person then has to add a new passkey on their device.
passkeyHelp.nameBody: This is the name people see when their device asks for a passkey, and the label their password manager saves. Keep it short. Changing it is safe and every passkey keeps working. A device that already saved one keeps showing the old name.

proxy.caption: Fetch feeds and article pages through a SOCKS5 or HTTP proxy.

proxy.directFallbackDesc: On by default — a proxy failure retries the fetch directly.

proxy.testFailed: Could not connect through the proxy: {{reason}}

info.directFallback: On by default. If the proxy fails, retry the fetch directly. Turn this off to keep your real server IP hidden — a proxy failure then fails the fetch instead of revealing your address.
info.remoteDns: Off by default. When on, the proxy is given the host name and resolves it, so your DNS resolver never sees which feeds you fetch and geo-restricted names resolve from the proxy’s location. Many SOCKS5 proxies do not resolve names at all — Private Internet Access is one — and answer every name with "host unreachable". Leave this off if the connection test fails that way.
info.piaCredentials: Private Internet Access needs a separately generated proxy username and password — not your account login.
